## Highlights since 0.20.0

- **Overleaf sync that comes back on its own.** In the native Lattice, Overleaf sync picks up again by itself after your Mac sleeps: the live connection counts the time asleep and joins again on wake, instead of leaving files at "Syncing is paused for this file". When the network changes under it, such as Wi-Fi to Ethernet or a VPN going up or down, Lattice checks the connection with a quick probe and joins again only if it has gone silent. An edit whose answer never comes on a silent connection ends that connection, and the edit is checked again on the new one. When Overleaf answers "too many requests", live sync waits out a cool-down instead of showing an error, and copies of Lattice that dropped together no longer all join again at the same moment.
- **Pause and resume Overleaf sync where you look.** In the native Lattice, while a project's sync is paused, the status bar reads Saved, sync paused, and its menu offers Resume syncing; on a syncing project it offers Pause syncing. The project menu and the command palette (⌘K) have Pause Overleaf sync and Resume Overleaf sync. Resuming syncs at once (in Manual mode it opens Review changes), and edits made on both sides while paused are merged, so nothing is overwritten.
- **Comment on Overleaf from the source editor.** In the native Lattice, in a project linked to Overleaf, Comment on Overleaf in the selection toolbar starts a comment on the passage that your co-authors see on Overleaf; Annotate still saves a note of your own. A saved note gets Share to Overleaf, which posts it as a comment on its passage, and a note's text can now be selected and copied (#1290).
- **Let the Agent work in the folder around your manuscript.** In the native Lattice, when you open a folder that holds one Lattice project, such as ProjectA with ProjectA/Manuscript inside, Lattice asks whether to open Manuscript with the whole folder available to the Agent, or to make the folder a project of its own. The first keeps the manuscript's one history and its builds where they are, and lets the Agent read the analysis scripts beside it. Settings › Agent › Display shows the choice under Agent’s folder and can undo it, and the project menu shows where History, Builds and the Agent work (#1293).
- **Coloured boxes and coloured text look as they print.** In the native Lattice's visual view, a `\colorbox` is drawn as one box that never breaks across lines, as in the PDF, instead of a highlight that wraps from line to line (#1327). Its visual Markdown editor shows inline text colours written as `<span style="color: …">`, so red and blue revisions stay visible, and saves them exactly as written (#831). In the source editor and a .tex file's visual view, text in `\textcolor` or after `\color` is drawn in its colour, made readable on light and dark themes (#1328).
- **A user guide for the native app, in English and Chinese.** The guide was checked against the native Lattice, grouped by task, given new screenshots and searchable in both languages. Help › User Guide opens it, and in the native Lattice opens the copy that comes with Lattice when the website can't be reached.

## Notable fixes

- Overleaf sync no longer risks replacing a file with an empty copy from Overleaf when your computer's clock is more than 10 minutes behind Overleaf's. Lattice now reads Overleaf's time from each answer and dates its own uploads by it. This applies to both the native and the classic app.
- In the native Lattice, the PDF stays sharp while you type at high zoom: past about 175% on a Retina screen, the live preview is drawn at full size instead of being stretched over the page.
- In the native Lattice's terminal, Tab and Shift+Tab go to the shell, so Tab completes a command instead of moving out of the terminal (#1272).
- The Agent's bundled runtime no longer re-reads old Claude Code transcripts every 30 seconds for its usage figures, which caused short bursts of high CPU for heavy Claude Code users (#1247).
- Confirmation dialogs that list many files, such as Overleaf's, now fit the window and scroll, so their buttons stay on screen.
- In the native Lattice, Add your first paper in an empty Papers panel opens Add papers (#1280).
- On Windows and Linux, reveal actions name the system's file manager instead of Finder, and the title bar no longer leaves room for the Mac's window buttons.
